title: How does the JVM find the matching catch block — using per-method exception table in bytecode — and why does a non-thrown try block have essentially ZERO runtime cost?
shortTitle: What is the JVM exception table?

s1_definition.profdef: The JVM does NOT use if-else or jump instructions for try-catch. Instead, each method has an **exception table** in its bytecode — a list of entries: `[try-start-PC, try-end-PC, handler-PC, caught-type]`. When an exception is thrown: the JVM checks the exception table for the current method — finds an entry where (1) the current PC is between try-start and try-end, (2) the thrown exception IS-A caught-type. If found → jump to handler-PC (the catch block). If NOT found → pop the current frame, repeat in the calling method (stack unwinding). **Zero cost when NO exception is thrown**: the try block is just normal bytecode — no extra branches, no overhead. The exception table is ONLY consulted when a throw actually happens. This means: try-catch is FREE on the happy path.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank doesn't post a guard at every door "just in case" (that would slow everything down). Instead, there's an EMERGENCY MANUAL in the office (exception table): "If fire alarm triggers between 9AM-5PM (try range), go to Exit B (handler). If between 5PM-9PM, go to Exit C." The manual sits unused during normal operation (ZERO cost). Only when the alarm rings (exception thrown) does someone consult it. Normal banking operations: ZERO slowdown from having emergency procedures.
s1_definition.oneliner: Exception table in bytecode: [start-PC, end-PC, handler-PC, type]. Try block: ZERO overhead when no exception thrown. Cost only on throw: table lookup + stack unwinding.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The JVM does NOT use if-else or jump instructions for try-catch. Instead, each method has an **exception table** in its bytecode — a list of entries: `[try-start-PC, try-end-PC, handler-PC, caught-type]`. When an exception is thrown: the JVM checks the exception table for the current method — finds an entry where (1) the current PC is between try-start and try-end, (2) the thrown exception IS-A caught-type. If found → jump to handler-PC (the catch block). If NOT found → pop the current frame, repeat in the calling method (stack unwinding). **Zero cost when NO exception is thrown**: the try block is just normal bytecode — no extra branches, no overhead. The exception table is ONLY consulted when a throw actually happens. This means: try-catch is FREE on the happy path.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank doesn't post a guard at every door "just in case" (that would slow everything down). Instead, there's an EMERGENCY MANUAL in the office (exception table): "If fire alarm triggers between 9AM-5PM (try range), go to Exit B (handler). If between 5PM-9PM, go to Exit C." The manual sits unused during normal operation (ZERO cost). Only when the alarm rings (exception thrown) does someone consult it. Normal banking operations: ZERO slowdown from having emergency procedures.

**One line to remember:** Exception table in bytecode: [start-PC, end-PC, handler-PC, type]. Try block: ZERO overhead when no exception thrown. Cost only on throw: table lookup + stack unwinding.

sections.s3_banking: Problem — the trade settlement service wraps its debit and credit logic in a try-catch, and a performance engineer worried that "all those try-catch blocks are slowing down our hot path." The team measured one million calls through the happy path and found the try-catch added no measurable cost. Fix: the JVM's per-method exception table is pure metadata — the try body runs as plain bytecode and the table is consulted ONLY when an exception is actually thrown, so wrapping settlement code in try-catch is free until something fails. This mini-project builds a small settlement-style method with two catch handlers and a JUnit test that proves the happy path with try-catch runs as fast as plain code.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean test
javap -c -v target/classes/com/bank/exceptiontable/ExceptionTableTest.class | grep -A5 "Exception table"
# Shows: from/to/target/type entries for each try-catch
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one million calls to `process("TRD-001")` on the happy path, plus a few calls with `"io"` and `"sql"` that trigger throws.

**Step 1.** On the happy path, execution enters the try body (bytecode PC 0 to 10), runs `settle(tradeId)`, and returns. The JVM never looks at the exception table — it is metadata sitting beside the method, not executable instructions — so there is no branch, no marker push, and no measurable overhead.

**Step 2.** When `"io"` is passed, an `IOException` is thrown at PC 1. Only now does the JVM consult the exception table for this method. It finds the entry `from=0 to=10 target=13 type=IOException`, confirms the thrown type IS-A IOException, and jumps to handler PC 13.

**Step 3.** When `"sql"` is passed, the first table entry (IOException) does not match, so the JVM checks the next entry `type=SQLException`, matches, and jumps to PC 20. If no entry matched, the JVM would pop this frame and repeat the search in the caller's exception table (stack unwinding).

**Step 4.** The performance test runs one million happy-path iterations with try-catch and one million of equivalent plain code; the two timings are nearly identical, proving the try block itself costs essentially zero.

```
INFO  2026-10-22T21:05:10 ExceptionTable withTry=12ms withoutTry=11ms (happy path ~ equal)
INFO  2026-10-22T21:05:10 ExceptionTable io->CAUGHT_IO sql->CAUGHT_SQL table consulted only on throw
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ JVM EXCEPTION TABLE ═══

  Method bytecode:
  PC  0: aload_1              ┐
  PC  1: invokevirtual settle │ TRY BODY (PC 0-10)
  PC 10: areturn              ┘ ← normal return, table NOT consulted!

  PC 13: astore_2             ┐ HANDLER 1 (IOException)
  PC 15: areturn              ┘

  PC 20: astore_2             ┐ HANDLER 2 (SQLException)
  PC 22: areturn              ┘

  Exception table:
  from=0  to=10  target=13  type=IOException
  from=0  to=10  target=20  type=SQLException

  ═══ HAPPY PATH: ZERO COST ═══
  PC 0 → 1 → 10 → return
  Exception table: NEVER consulted! Just metadata.

  ═══ EXCEPTION PATH ═══
  PC 0 → 1 → THROW! → consult table → match IOException → jump PC 13
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │     PAYMENT SERVICE — BYTECODE EXECUTION VIEW (JVM)        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   REST Controller ──► PaymentService.transfer()
                             │
                             ▼
            ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
            │  try { debit(); credit(); }      │  ← happy path =
            │  catch(SQLException e){ rollback }│    PLAIN bytecode
            └──────────────────────────────────┘    (table = metadata)
                             │ throw only on failure
                             ▼
              [JVM consults per-method exception table → handler PC]
   Takeaway: try-catch = 0 cost until THROW; never use for control flow
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM uses a per-method exception table in the bytecode — not if-else or branch instructions. Each entry maps a PC range (try body) to a handler PC (catch block) for a specific exception type. When no exception is thrown, the try body executes as PLAIN bytecode with ZERO overhead — the table is metadata, never consulted on the happy path. This means: wrapping code in try-catch costs NOTHING on the normal execution path.

Cost only appears when an exception is actually THROWN: fillInStackTrace() walks the stack (~2μs), the JVM looks up the exception table (fast), and unwinds frames until a matching handler is found. This is why try-catch is free but THROWING is expensive — and why you should never use exceptions for control flow (the throw cost adds up).

keyPoints: Per-method bytecode table mapping: try range, catch type, handler offset
try block has ZERO runtime cost — no instructions added for entering try
Cost is only on throw: JVM walks the exception table to find handler
This is why try-catch is cheap but exceptions are expensive to throw
